newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian barley returns forecast to fall - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: Australian barley returns forecast to fall - ABARE.

text.p: Australian barley returns are expected to fall in 1997/98 due to high carryover stocks from last year's record crop and strong international competition, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said in its June quarter report.
Average gross unit returns are expected to fall by A$10 to A$135 a tonne for feed barley, with returns for malting barley forecast to drop A$18 to A$162 a tonne, it said.
As a result, Australian barley plantings are forecast to fall in 1997/98 reflecting grower intentions to switch to higher earning crops.
ABARE said the smaller area planted and expectations of below average yields meant that barley production was forecast to be down almost 40 percent to around 4.12 million tonnes.

Australian coarse grain production is expected to be down 26 percent to 7.6 million tonnes, with exports down 40 percent to 3.1 million tonnes and export value down almost 50 percent to A$586 million, it said.
ABARE said world corn prices are forecast to ease in 1997/98 as production remains at near record levels and stocks continued to recover.
Feed barley prices are also expected to ease as competition from corn intensifies and the European Union increases subsidised exports to several key markets.
ABARE said that reflecting lower barley and sorghum plantings, world coarse grains production is forecast to be 879 million tonnes, one percent below the record 1996/97 harvest.

World corn production is forecast to be 565 million tonnes in 1997/98, around seven million tonnes down on 1996/97, reflecting return to average yields in the United States and the impact of excessively dry conditions through Europe.
World barley production is forecast to fall by two percent in 1997/98, driven by reduced production in Europe and Canada, it said.
ABARE said world coarse grain consumption is forecast to rise almost one percent in 1997/98 to 878 million tonnes through continued growth in livestock feed demand, particularly in Asia.

From an Australian perspective, it said China is forecast to continue to be a significant growth market for malting barley in 1997/98, while import demand for feed barley from Saudi Arabia is expected to continue its upward trend, it said.
However, ABARE said Australia will continue to face strong competition from subsidised European Union exports of feed barley and processed malt.
